June 23, 2006
ORDER
ROBERT C. LEWIS, : NV-04-01-03
:
Appellant : Grazing
:
v. : Appeal from Assistant Field Manager’s
: Final Decision dated July 30, 2001,
BUREAU OF LAND MANAGEMENT, : involving the Henrie Complex, Breedlove
: and Grapevine Allotments, Ely Field
Respondent : Office, Nevada
PARTIALLY GRANTING MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGEMENT
GRANTING MOTION TO PARTIALLY VACATE
I. Introduction
This matter is before me on the motions of the Bureau of Land Management (1) to
dismiss; or, alternatively, for summary judgement, dated May 19, 2006; and, (2) to partially
remand, dated June 5, 2006, as modified by a motion to vacate, dated June 7, 2006. The current
record allows me to partially grant BLM’s motion for summary judgement and to grant its
motion to vacate.
Appellant, Robert C. Lewis, has stated three reasons why he believes the BLM grazing
decision is wrong. His first reason, that the decision wrongly reduces his total AUM’s, allotment
acreage and seasons of use, cannot be sustained because the BLM decision correctly implements
a management framework plan which I do not have jurisdiction to review. However, Lewis’s
second reason, that the decision wrongly reduces his total AUM’s because his land is not 100%
fenced, can be sustained because BLM has effectively admitted error in that part of the decision.
But, a hearing must be conducted on his third reason, that the decision provides for inadequate
fencing, because the record does not now contain the facts necessary to resolve this claim.
II. Background
BLM’s motions seek to resolve each of the reasons stated by Lewis for overturning its
July 30, 2001 decision. This decision implemented the provisions of the 2000 Caliente
Management Framework Plan (“MFP”) Amendment which required changes to the terms of

NV-04-01-03
several livestock grazing permits in order to assist the recovery of the desert tortise, a threatened
species under the Endangered Species Act. 1/ The amendment created three Areas of Critical
Environmental Concern (“ACEC”) and required specific changes to livestock grazing
management within them. Lewis filed a protest of the MFP Amendment, which BLM did not
consider because it was filed late. 2/ When BLM later issued its decision implementing the MFP
Amendments on the three allotments permitted to Lewis (the Breedlove, Grapevine, and Henrie
Complex Allotments), he filed a timely appeal.
The appeal filed by Lewis consists of a single page. It states the following three reasons
why he thinks the BLM decision is wrong:
1. “This decision causes adverse economic conditions in my cattle grazing operation due
to reduction in total Aums [sic.], allotment acreage, and seasons of use.”
2. “Furthermore, this final decision cuts the total Aums [sic.], and says that my private
property is 100% fenced.”
3. “This final decision disallows me from using portions of my existing allotments
without providing adequate fencing to keep my cattle out of the ACEC.” 3/
The following discussion addresses each of these reasons in turn.
III. Discussion
A. Reduction of AUMs, Allotment Acreage, and Seasons of Use.
Lewis’s first ground for appeal cannot be granted because BLM’s decision correctly
implements the MFP Amendment. The Amendment specifically eliminated grazing within the
three ACECs and reduced the associated AUMs. 4/ The Amendment also specified the seasons

of use and AUMs for grazing outside of the ACECs. 5/ BLM’s implementing decision required
changes to Lewis’s existing permits that tracks the MFP Amendments on these details. 6/ Lewis
has not pointed out any specific variances.
The Board of Land Appeals has held that it does not have authority to review BLM
decisions to approve or amend a resource management plan. 7/ The Board reasoned that because
a resource management plan “establishes management policy, its approval is subject only to
protest to the Director, BLM, whose decision is final for the Department.” 8/ Because a
management framework plan is a type of resource management plan 9/ the same rule applies to
the MFP Amendment in this case. Further, because the Board’s reasoning applies with equal
force to the Hearings Division, it follows that the Hearings Division also does not have authority
to review a management plan. Thus, I must conclude that the MFP Amendment may not be
reviewed in this proceeding.
However, the Board has also made clear that a difference exists between a management
plan and an implementation decision. A BLM decision implementing a management plan may
be reviewed while a management plan cannot. 10/ Accordingly, I may review the BLM decision
of July 30, 2001, but not the MFP Amendment of 2000. Because Lewis seeks review of the
BLM implementing decision, that portion of BLM’s motion which seeks to dismiss the appeal
for lack of jurisdiction must be denied because authority does exist for review of implementing
decisions.
Even though dismissal of Lewis’s appeal for lack of jurisdiction is not appropriate, I do
have authority to dispose of the appeal on a motion for summary judgement. A summary
judgment may be granted where “there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and * * * the

moving party is entitled to judgement as a matter of law.” 11/ BLM points out that regulations
require it to manager livestock grazing “in accordance with applicable land use plans” and that
the grazing activities it approves and the management actions it takes must conform to such
plans. 12/ BLM argues that Lewis’s appeal must be denied because BLM’s implementing
decision conforms to the MFP Amendment.
An appellant, such as Lewis, must support an appeal by “argument or evidence” that
establishes error by the standard of a preponderance of the evidence. 13/ In responding to BLM’s
motions, Lewis has not shown that BLM failed to follow the mandates of the MFP Amendment.
He has not pointed to any instance where BLM incorrectly applied the Amendment’s reduction
of AUMs, allotment acreage, or seasons of use to his three allotments. Rather he has alleged a
broad range of new reasons why the BLM erred. He claims that the BLM decision covers
property that is not public land, excludes him from accessing and using his land, denies him his
vested water rights, and denies him the use of preexisting rights-of way, among other grounds.
14/ He did not clearly state any of these grounds in the document he filed as his appeal in 2001.
15/
Regulations specifically require an appellant to state clearly why he or she believes a
BLM decision is wrong at the time an appeal is filed. Further, any ground for appeal not
included in the appeal is waived:
The appeal shall state the reasons, clearly and concisely, why the appellant thinks
the final decision * * * is in error. All grounds for error not stated shall be
considered as waived, and no such waived ground of error may be presented at the
hearing unless ordered or permitted by the administrative law judge. 16/
11/ See Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c). The Board of Land Appeals has recognized the use of
summary judgement procedures in administrative procedures. See Larson v. Bureau of Land
Management, 129 IBLA 250, 252 (1994).
12/ 43 CFR 4100.0-8 (2000).
13/ See Leonard J. Olheiser, 106 IBLA 214, 216 (1988).
14/ Appellants’ Answer to BLM’s Motion to Dismiss; Motion for Summary Judgement;
and Motion for Expedited Ruling, dated June 6, 2006.
15/ Letter, dated August 21, 2001, from Robert C. Lewis to “BLM, Ely Field Office.”
16/ 43 CFR 4.470(a) (2000).

Lewis did not include in his appeal the reasons for error which he now uses to oppose BLM’s
motions and he has not presented a compelling reason why he should now be permitted to
present them. Because the regulations provide that all grounds not stated in the appeal are
waived, I must decline to permit Lewis to raise them at this stage of the proceedings.
Therefore BLM’s motion should be granted on Lewis’s first ground for appeal because
Lewis has not shown that BLM erred. The BLM’s implementing decision followed the terms
mandated by the MFP Amendment. Since explicit regulations require BLM to follow these
mandates, it did not commit error when it included them in its implementing decision.
Accordingly BLM is entitled to a conclusion in its favor as a matter of law.
B. Reduction in Credit for Private Land
Lewis’s second ground for appeal states that the BLM erred because the “final decision
cuts the total Aums [sic.], and says that my private property is 100% fenced.” BLM has
addressed this issue in two motions. It first moved to remand that part of the decision which
changed the percent of Federal land in the Breedlove allotment from 90% to 100% based on a
finding that Lewis’s private land was 100% fenced. The basis for the motion stemmed from a
recent investigation finding that at least a portion of the base property was not fenced. 17/ I
denied that motion because BLM appeared to reserve the option of affirming its original decision
after it conducted further investigation. 18/ BLM subsequently filed a new motion explicitly
seeking to vacate the part of the decision it originally sought to remand. 19/
The two motions have the practical effect of admitting that BLM erred in finding that
Lewis’s land was 100% fenced. Correction of the error requires acceptance of the prior permit’s
conclusion that the Breedlove allotment encompassed 90% federal land. 20/ A conclusion that
the allotment consisted of 90% federal land (and by implication 10% private land) means that a
total of 78 AUMs (698 AUMs (permitted by the MFP Amendments) x .10/.90 = 78 AUMs) are

contributed by Lewis’s unfenced private land. 21/ Thus, the “Permitted Use Active AUMs” on
the Breedlove allotment must be increased from the 698 22/ stated in the decision to a revised
number of 776. 23/
Lewis has formally opposed granting BLM’s motion to vacate by making many of the
same arguments he advanced in opposition to BLM’s motion for summary judgement. 24/
Because he did not clearly state these grounds when he filed his appeal, they are deemed waived
and will not be further considered here. 25/ More importantly, Lewis has not stated a persuasive
reason why BLM should be prevented from vacating that part of the decision it no longer desires
to support. Lewis appealed on the ground that BLM erred in stating that his private lands were
100% fenced. BLM has now acknowledged that it was wrong and has acceded to correcting the
decision. This result provides the remedy due Lewis for a successful appeal on this ground.
Accordingly, that portion of the decision concluding that the Breedlove allotment
contains 100 “Percent Federal Land” can be vacated and corrected to show 90 “Percent Federal
Land” (the same as in the prior permit); and, that portion of the decision concluding that the
“Permitted Use Active AUMs” in the Breedlove allotment is 698 can be vacated and corrected to
show that “Permitted Use Active AUMs” is 776. 26/ In effect, Lewis is granted a finding and
conclusion in his favor on this ground for appeal.
Nothing in this finding and conclusion should be construed as permitting BLM to revise
or affirm its original decision within the context of this appeal. If BLM later decides that the
Breedlove allotment is not 90 “Percent Federal Land,” it should issue an appropriate decision
with applicable appeal rights.

C. Failure to Provide for Fencing
Lewis lastly claims that the “decision disallows me from using portions of my existing
allotments without providing adequate fencing to keep my cattle out of the ACEC.” I partially
addressed this reason for appeal in an Order Limiting Issues for Hearing, dated June 16, 2006.
BLM's motion seeks to dismiss this reason by arguing that Lewis has no standing since
BLM has taken no action on a fence construction application. However, BLM's argument
ignores the provision of the MFP Amendment that requires construction of improvements to
exclude livestock from the ACECs. The MFP Amendment specifies the following requirement
on page 13:
Construct improvements only as needed to facilitate multiple use and to exclude
livestock from the Kane Springs, Mormon Mesa, and Beaver Dam Slope ACECs.
I can find no provision in the BLM decision which implements this requirement.
However, I cannot now decide the merits of this ground for appeal because it requires fact
findings that I cannot make from the record before me. Such findings include: the location of
existing fences in relationship to ACEC boundaries, the need for fences to keep livestock out of
the ACECs, and the person who should build fences if required. Therefore, BLM’s motion for
summary judgement on this reason must be denied.
IV. Conclusion
Accordingly, for good cause, it is ordered that:
1. The motion of the Bureau of Land Management to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction is
denied.
2. The alternative motion of the Bureau of Land Management for summary judgement is
partially granted and partially denied.
3. The portion of the Bureau of Land Management’s motion for summary judgement that
seeks dismissal of the following reason why the Final Decision, dated July 30, 2001, is wrong is
granted and, accordingly, this ground for Lewis’s appeal is dismissed.
“This decision causes adverse economic conditions in my cattle grazing operation
due to reduction in total Aums [sic.], allotment acreage, and seasons of use.”
4. The Bureau of Land Management’s motion to partially vacate is granted
